o1.biggest_strength: A dated, staged plan with real gates (data check, 8-week new-visitor test, launch, 90-day read) that respects the 12-month promise and never touches an existing bill.
o1.biggest_mistake: The break-even is misstated: on its own mid case the plan stays profitable down to about 1 in 4.8 Team 8+ downgrades (roughly 21%), not 1 in 6, so the stop rule would kill a profitable plan; the LTV comparison also mixes prices ($690 at $66 vs $1,950 at $80) and the $41k 'first five months' contradicts the $57k six-month figure in the table.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Get the break-even and LTV arithmetic right, and instead of dismissing the yearly lever on a confused payback argument, quantify it (0.9% vs 4.0% churn, cash collected up front) and fold it into the plan.

o2.biggest_strength: Every number traces and ties: $2.21M total, Essentials 8+ at $249k (11% of revenue) but 29% of churned revenue, blended $76.53 Agency price, and a correctly derived break-even at about 1 in 3 Team downgrades.
o2.biggest_mistake: It under-specifies sequencing and dates around the test (no start date, and an 8-week window is thin for reading 5-6% monthly churn), and the 2-user allowance plus approvals invites more Team cannibalisation than the 1-user guard it replaced.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add the dated stage gates (data check, test start/end, launch, 90-day read) with the same discipline it applies to the numbers, and say what the 15-channel cliff does to a 16-channel Agency customer.

reason: Both pick the right target and the right shape, but output 2's arithmetic survives checking line by line — including the 29%-of-churn framing and the correct 1-in-3 break-even — while output 1's headline stop rule rests on a wrong break-even and it waves away the yearly-billing lever the data most clearly points to. Output 2 also literally uses our 'Here's exactly what you'd pay' line and keeps claims honest; it needs only dates and a slightly tighter test window before I'd run it.
